title: Joshua 19:32–39
context: The sixth lot falls to Naphtali, in the far north near the sea of Chinnereth (Galilee), with a list of fortified cities that includes Hazor and Kedesh. Hazor had been the head of the northern kingdoms that Joshua defeated (Joshua 11:10), and Kedesh would later be named as a city of refuge (Joshua 20:7). As with Zebulun, later Scripture speaks of this region as the land where God would bring light, fulfilled in Jesus’ ministry in Galilee (Isaiah 9:1–2; Matthew 4:13–16). Readers in both traditions commonly treat these verses as shared ground on God’s gift of land and his long-range purposes for the northern tribes. Many places in the list cannot be located with certainty.

verses.text: The sixth lot came out for the children of Naphtali, even for the children of Naphtali according to their families.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that the sixth lot comes out for Naphtali according to their families. God’s ordering continues as the northern tribes receive their portions.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the lot again as God’s chosen means of distribution. Both traditions commonly read the verse as part of the steady fulfillment of God’s promise.

verses.text: Their border was from Heleph, from the oak in Zaanannim, Adami-nekeb, and Jabneel, to Lakkum. It ended at the Jordan.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the border beginning at Heleph and the oak in Zaanannim and ending at the Jordan. The inheritance is traced through real landmarks.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the detailed boundary as testimony to the concreteness of God’s gift. The exact positions of several landmarks are uncertain, and readers in both traditions commonly hold them with caution.

verses.text: The border turned westward to Aznoth Tabor, and went out from there to Hukkok. It reached to Zebulun on the south, and reached to Asher on the west, and to Judah at the Jordan toward the sunrise.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that Naphtali’s border touches Zebulun, Asher and the Jordan, fitting together with neighboring tribes. The phrase to Judah at the Jordan is difficult, and interpreters explain it in more than one way.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the difficulty of the reference to Judah while affirming the overall picture of interlocking tribal territories. Both traditions commonly read the verse as showing God’s ordered distribution among his people.

verses.text: The fortified cities were Ziddim, Zer, Hammath, Rakkath, Chinnereth,
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers notice the list of fortified cities, including Chinnereth near the sea that later bears the name of Galilee. Naphtali received strong towns as part of its inheritance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the fortified cities as part of God’s generous provision. Readers in both traditions commonly note that this region later became the center of Jesus’ ministry (Matthew 4:13).

verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers notice Hazor, once the head of the northern kingdoms that opposed Israel (Joshua 11:10). A former center of opposition becomes part of Israel’s inheritance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s victory over Hazor issuing in its inclusion among Naphtali’s towns. Both traditions commonly see this as an example of God turning conquest into settled inheritance.

verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers notice Kedesh, which will be named as a city of refuge in the next chapter (Joshua 20:7). Naphtali’s inheritance includes a place of mercy for all Israel.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the inclusion of Kedesh as linking tribal inheritance with God’s provision of refuge. Readers in both traditions commonly see the connection as part of the coherence of God’s gifts.

verses.text: Iron, Migdal El, Horem, Beth Anath, and Beth Shemesh; nineteen cities with their villages.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note the summary of nineteen cities with their villages. As with other tribes, the total and the names do not obviously align, a feature interpreters handle in different ways.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the count as part of the faithful record of God’s gift, held with humility where details are unclear. Both traditions commonly note that Judges 1:33 records Naphtali living among the Canaanites in Beth Shemesh and Beth Anath.

verses.text: This is the inheritance of the tribe of the children of Naphtali according to their families, the cities with their villages.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the closing formula confirming Naphtali’s inheritance by families. The pattern underscores God’s care for each household.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the summary as marking the completeness of God’s gift to Naphtali. Readers in both traditions commonly connect this region with the later hope of light dawning in Galilee (Isaiah 9:1–2).
